<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{jingquan.yan,yuwei.miao,peiran.yu,jzhuang}@uta.edu</span></a>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Attention-based regression models are often trained by jointly optimizing Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss and Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) loss, emphasizing the magnitude of errors and the order or shape of targets, respectively. A common but poorly understood phenomenon during training is the <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PCC plateau</em>: PCC stops improving early in training, even as MSE continues to decrease. We provide the first rigorous theoretical analysis of this behavior, revealing fundamental limitations in both optimization dynamics and model capacity. First, in regard to the flattened PCC curve, we uncover a critical conflict where lowering MSE (magnitude matching) can <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">paradoxically</em> suppress the PCC gradient (shape matching). This issue is exacerbated by the softmax attention mechanism, particularly when the data to be aggregated is highly homogeneous. Second, we identify a limitation in the model capacity: we derived a PCC improvement limit for <em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">any</em> convex aggregator (including the softmax attention), showing that the convex hull of the inputs strictly bounds the achievable PCC gain. We demonstrate that data homogeneity intensifies both limitations. Motivated by these insights, we propose the Extrapolative Correlation Attention (ECA), which incorporates novel, theoretically-motivated mechanisms to improve the PCC optimization and extrapolate beyond the convex hull. Across diverse benchmarks, including challenging homogeneous data setting, ECA consistently breaks the PCC plateau, achieving significant improvements in correlation without compromising MSE performance.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">

<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The attention mechanism is a powerful tool for regression tasks where each input sample comprises multiple elements, such as tokens or image patches, and the elements’ embeddings are aggregated using attention mechanism to predict a continuous target <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martins et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Born and Manica, 2023</a>)</cite>. This paradigm is widely used in areas like digital pathology, time-series prediction and emotional analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. For example, in video-based sentiment analysis, the attention mechanism is used to aggregate frame embeddings within a video clip to predict emotion variables, such as sentiment intensity, arousal, and valence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Truong and Lauw, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Two characteristics are common in such applications. First, the in-sample data frequently exhibits <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">higher homogeneity</span> than cross-sample data. For example, in pathology images, nearby regions tend to share more similar tissue or cell types than distant regions. Likewise, in video-based sentiment analysis, frames from the same clip are more similar than frames from different clips. Second, the regression performance is not simply evaluated by <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">magnitude</span> (e.g., Mean Squared Error (MSE)) but also by <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">shape</span>—the relative ordering of predictions, measured by the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC). In many settings, capturing the correct correlations matters more than predicting the exact values <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pandit and Schuller, 2019</a>)</cite>. For instance, in spatial transcriptomics, capturing the relative trend of gene expression (<em id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, co-expression) is more informative than predicting exact magnitudes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. To emphasize shape while retaining magnitude performance, models are commonly trained with a joint loss function, such as <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L_{\text{total}}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>total</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>MSE</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L_{\text{total}}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is the PCC and <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{PCC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{PCC}}</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyperparameter weight <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>(a) Illustration of a video-based sentiment analysis example. A sample is considered homogeneous when its within-sample dispersion <math id="S1.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\sigma}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\sigma}</annotation></semantics></math> is below <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. (b) A convex attention yields an aggregated embedding inside the convex hull of the sample’s embeddings. (C) Our ECA extrapolates beyond the hull to amplify within-sample contrasts.</figcaption><img src="2602.17898v1/figure_1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/144;" width="548" height="144" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, such joint training strategy applied to attention-based regression model frequently exhibits a puzzling <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">PCC plateau</em>, even with large PCC weight <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{PCC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{PCC}}</annotation></semantics></math>. As shown in <a href="#S1.F2" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the PCC curve’s slope flattens early in training, failing to improve further even while the MSE continues to decrease. This empirical phenomenon is particularly severe with high in-sample homogeneity data. The underlying mechanisms driving this plateau remain unclear and it raises a critical question: why does the regression model fail to optimize the correlation effectively?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we provide the first theoretical investigation into this question, analyzing the limitations of standard attention from two distinct perspectives: <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimization dynamics</span> and <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">model capacity</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:47%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17898v1/PCC_plateau_temp.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/125;" width="264" height="125"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>PCC plateau example: PCC flattens at early epoch while MSE continues to decrease. The plateau becomes more noticeable as within-sample homogeneity increases, specifically, dataset A is more homogeneous than B.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitation 1: Conflict in Optimization Dynamics.</span>
Our analysis reveals a direct relation between the decrease of MSE and the flattening of the PCC curve in the attention-based regression model. Using a decomposition of MSE (<a href="#S2.Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 2.1 (MSE Mean–std–correlation Decomposition). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>), we show the following. Although training continues to reduce MSE by matching the predictions’ mean and standard deviation, the gradient of the correlation term is paradoxically attenuated, flattening the PCC curve. This effect is amplified by <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in-sample homogeneity</em>: when embeddings within a sample are similar, the within-sample dispersion term in the PCC gradient shrinks and further suppresses the magnitude of the gradient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Limitation 2: Model Capacity of Convex Aggregation.</span>
Notice that softmax attention is a convex combination of element embeddings; we compare convex attention aggregation to mean-pooling aggregation and derive an upper bound on the achievable PCC gain (<a href="#S2.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2.2 (PCC Gain Bound for Convex Attention). ‣ Prediction Decompositon. ‣ 2.4 Model Capacity: The PCC Ceiling of Convex Aggregation ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Theorem</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) depending on the radius of convex hull formed by the in-sample embeddings. Greater in-sample homogeneity will shrink the convex hull and tightens this bound, yielding a fundamental capacity limit for PCC gain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extrapolative Correlation Attention.</span>
Motivated by these theoretical insights, we propose Extrapolative Correlation Attention (ECA), a novel framework designed to overcome these limitations. To mitigate the optimization conflict in Limitation 1, ECA introduces a Dispersion-Normalized PCC loss to counteracts the attenuation effect, restoring the magnitude of correlation gradient. We also employ Dispersion-Aware Temperature Softmax to prevent the gradient collapse and near-uniform attention distribution under in-sample homogeneity. To address Limitation 2, ECA introduces Scaled Residual Aggregation, which allows the model to extrapolate beyond the convex hull, mitigating the PCC gain limitation induced by convex aggregation mechanism.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span>
We theoretically investigate the PCC plateau when training attention-based regression model with a joint MSE+PCC loss. We identify two limitations in optimization dynamics and in model capacity.</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimization Dynamics.</span> We identify a conflict in optimization dynamics: as MSE optimization increases <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> to match <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math>, the magnitude of the PCC loss gradient scales with <math id="S1.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> leading to a flattened PCC curve during training. In addition, We show that within-sample homogeneity further shrinks the PCC gradient through the Jacobian of softmax attention. Both parts contribute to the PCC plateau phenomenon.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Capacity.</span> We prove that for any convex aggregator (<em id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, softmax attention), the achievable PCC improvement over mean-pooling can be bounded by the within-sample data homogeneity.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To address these limitations, we introduce ECA, a novel attention-based regression framework with three components:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the optimization limitation, we re-scale the PCC objective to counteract the <math id="S1.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> factor, restoring correlation gradients magnitude while minimizing MSE.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the convex aggregator limitation, we incorporate a Scaled Residual Aggregation that enables controlled extrapolation beyond the convex hull.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To handle within-sample homogeneity, we propose a Dispersion-Aware Temperature Softmax to prevent attention collapse and amplify the informative contrasts within homogeneous samples.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Across diverse regression benchmarks, ECA consistently overcomes the PCC plateau and achieves higher correlation gains while maintaining competitive MSE. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We theoretically analyze why the PCC plateau occurs when training attention-based regression with a joint MSE+PCC loss. First, we relate MSE and PCC through a decomposition that motivates joint training. Then we prove that softmax attention, as a convex aggregator, limits both the optimization dynamics and the model’s expressive capacity. These limits hinder correlation learning and explain the observed PCC plateau.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Problem Setup</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Notation.</span>
We consider a regression dataset with a batch of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> samples <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{s},y_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{s},y_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>. Each sample <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> is a set of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> element with embeddings <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{s}=\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{s}=\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{si}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{si}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{s},\hat{y}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{s},\hat{y}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> be the ground-truth target and model prediction for <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{\text{th}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mtext>th</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{\text{th}}</annotation></semantics></math> sample. The batch-level empirical means are <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{y},\mu_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{y},\mu_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> and standard deviations are <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y},\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y},\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Define centered targets and predictions as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{s}:=y_{s}-\mu_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{s}:=y_{s}-\mu_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{s}:=\hat{y}_{s}-\mu_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{s}:=\hat{y}_{s}-\mu_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attention-based Aggregation.</span>
The attention-based model processes each input sample to produce a scalar prediction. An attention scoring function <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{attn}}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>attn</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{attn}}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> (<em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, KQV dot-product similarity or gating mechanism) scores each embedding in <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> and produces attention logits <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}_{s}=f_{\text{attn}}(\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{s}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>attn</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}_{s}=f_{\text{attn}}(\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}_{i=1}^{n_{s}})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{s}}</annotation></semantics></math> with entries <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{si}=[\mathbf{z}_{s}]_{i}\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{si}=[\mathbf{z}_{s}]_{i}\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>. Softmax converts these logits to positive attention weights <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\alpha}_{s}=\operatorname{Softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝜶</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>Softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐳</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\alpha}_{s}=\operatorname{Softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{s})</annotation></semantics></math> on the probability simplex with entries <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha_{si}=[\bm{\alpha}_{s}]_{i}\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>𝜶</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha_{si}=[\bm{\alpha}_{s}]_{i}\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\alpha_{si}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\alpha_{si}=1</annotation></semantics></math>. The sample-level embedding is the convex combination <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\alpha_{si}\,\mathbf{h}_{si}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{s}}\alpha_{si}\,\mathbf{h}_{si}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, a linear regression head with weights <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> and bias <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> produces the scalar prediction: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}_{s}=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{s}+c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}_{s}=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{s}+c</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that this formulation is backbone-agnostic: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{h}_{si}\}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the features at the final layer of any deep architecture (<em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, a multi-layer Transformer). Since these models typically derive the final prediction with a convex attention pooling (<em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g.</em>, [CLS] token aggregation) followed by a linear projection, our analysis of the attention-based aggregation and its interaction with joint MSE and PCC optimization applies regardless of the depth or complexity of the preceding backbone. We provide a detailed discussion on the applicability to deep architectures in <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Generality of Theoretical Analysis Regarding Architecture Depth ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning Objective.</span> We measure Pearson correlation between targets and predictions over the batch by
<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho:=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})}{\sigma_{\mathbf{y}}\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>Cov</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>𝐲</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho:=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})}{\sigma_{\mathbf{y}}\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To optimize both magnitude and correlation of the prediction, we use the popular joint loss
<math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}:=\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>total</mtext></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>MSE</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}:=\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{PCC}}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{PCC}}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> balances the two terms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Homogeneity Measures.</span> For each sample, let the in-sample mean be
<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\mu}_{s}=\tfrac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{s}}\mathbf{h}_{sj}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\mu}_{s}=\tfrac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{s}}\mathbf{h}_{sj}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We quantify within-sample homogeneity by (i) the in-sample dispersion
<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{s}=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{s}}\lVert\mathbf{h}_{sj}-\bm{\mu}_{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{s}=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{s}}\lVert\mathbf{h}_{sj}-\bm{\mu}_{s}\rVert_{2}^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and (ii) the convex-hull radius
<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{s}:=\max_{i}\lVert\mathbf{h}_{si}-\bm{\mu}_{s}\rVert_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em">⁡</mo><msub><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">∥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{s}:=\max_{i}\lVert\mathbf{h}_{si}-\bm{\mu}_{s}\rVert_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These quantities are related by inequality <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{s}\leq R_{s}\leq\sqrt{n_{s}}\,\sigma_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msqrt><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{s}\leq R_{s}\leq\sqrt{n_{s}}\,\sigma_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> with proof in <a href="#A4.Thmlemma3" title="Lemma D.3 (Dispersion–Radius Connection). ‣ D.2 Connection between In-sample Dispersion and Radius ‣ Appendix D Achievable PCC Bound of Convex Attention Models ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.
Cross-sample homogeneity is summarized by the root-mean-square (RMS) values
<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\sigma}:=\big(\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sigma_{s}^{2}\big)^{1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>σ</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>:=</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>S</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\sigma}:=\big(\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\sigma_{s}^{2}\big)^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{R}:=\big(\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}R_{s}^{2}\big)^{1/2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>:=</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>S</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>S</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{R}:=\big(\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}R_{s}^{2}\big)^{1/2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC</h3>

<div id="S2.Thmproposition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmproposition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmproposition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(MSE Mean–std–correlation Decomposition)<span id="S2.Thmproposition1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmproposition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmproposition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmproposition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The MSE between <math id="S2.Thmproposition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmproposition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{y}</annotation></semantics></math> can be decomposed as:</span></p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\underbrace{(\mu_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}-\mu_{\mathbf{y}})^{2}}_{\text{mean matching}}+\underbrace{(\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}-\sigma_{\mathbf{y}})^{2}}_{\text{std matching}}+\underbrace{2\,\sigma_{\mathbf{y}}\,\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}\,\bigl(1-\rho\bigr)}_{\text{weighted correlation}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>MSE</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>𝐲</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">mean matching</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>𝐲</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">std matching</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>𝐲</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐲</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">weighted correlation</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\operatorname{MSE}(\mathbf{y},\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\underbrace{(\mu_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}-\mu_{\mathbf{y}})^{2}}_{\text{mean matching}}+\underbrace{(\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}-\sigma_{\mathbf{y}})^{2}}_{\text{std matching}}+\underbrace{2\,\sigma_{\mathbf{y}}\,\sigma_{\hat{\mathbf{y}}}\,\bigl(1-\rho\bigr)}_{\text{weighted correlation}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmlemma1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmlemma1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Scaling-invariance of PCC)<span id="S2.Thmlemma1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>.
<math id="S2.Thmlemma1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{PCC}(y,m\hat{y}+n)=\operatorname{PCC}(y,\hat{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>PCC</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>PCC</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{PCC}(y,m\hat{y}+n)=\operatorname{PCC}(y,\hat{y})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We defer the proof for <a href="#S2.Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 2.1 (MSE Mean–std–correlation Decomposition). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S2.Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 2.1 (Scaling-invariance of PCC). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> to <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Preliminaries ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmremark1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmremark1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmremark1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmremark1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmremark1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S2.Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 2.1 (MSE Mean–std–correlation Decomposition). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Propositions</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a><span id="S2.Thmremark1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> and <a href="#S2.Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 2.1 (Scaling-invariance of PCC). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> are model-independent and hold for any regressor.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmremark2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmremark2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 2.2</span></span><span id="S2.Thmremark2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(The PCC Plateau)<span id="S2.Thmremark2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmremark2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.Thmremark2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmremark2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">By <a href="#S2.Thmproposition1" title="Proposition 2.1 (MSE Mean–std–correlation Decomposition). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Proposition</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, minimizing MSE jointly targets (i) mean matching, (ii) standard deviation matching, and (iii) weighted correlation. Because MSE is sensitive to affine transformations while PCC is invariant (<a href="#S2.Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 2.1 (Scaling-invariance of PCC). ‣ 2.2 Preliminaries: The Interplay Between MSE and PCC ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Lemma</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>), optimization can reduce MSE by mainly adjusting mean and scale, with little improvement on correlation. This explains why MSE may keep decreasing while PCC plateaus, and motivates adding the explicit correlation term <math id="S2.Thmremark2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">PCC</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)</annotation></semantics></math> to the objective.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The discussion above provides intuitions for the PCC plateau phenomenon. We further empirically validate this phenomenon on 8 UCI regression datasets using multi-layer Transformers (<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Extended Empirical Evidence of the PCC Plateau ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>). <a href="#A6.F7" title="In Appendix F Extended Empirical Evidence of the PCC Plateau ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows a consistent pattern across all tasks: PCC curve flattens before MSE convergence. This consistent pattern confirms that “PCC plateau” is a general correlation learning failure mode under attention-based joint optimization setting. We now provide a formal analysis by characterizing the PCC gradient in attention-based regression models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Optimization Dynamics: The Correlation Gradient Bottleneck</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study how the gradients propagate through the attention aggregator when optimizing the joint loss <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>total</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>MSE</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mtext>PCC</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}+\lambda_{\text{PCC}}(1-\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>. We derive the gradients of both MSE and PCC with respect to the attention logits <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{si}</annotation></semantics></math> to understand the optimization dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmlemma2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 2.2</span></span><span id="S2.Thmlemma2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Softmax Aggregator Jacobian)<span id="S2.Thmlemma2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The derivative of the aggregated embedding <math id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to a pre-softmax logit <math id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{si}</annotation></semantics></math> is
<math id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial\mathbf{v}_{s}/\partial z_{si}=\alpha_{si}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mphantom></mphantom><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial\mathbf{v}_{s}/\partial z_{si}=\alpha_{si}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})</annotation></semantics></math> and
consequently, <math id="S2.Thmlemma2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\partial\hat{y}_{s}/\partial z_{si}=\alpha_{si}\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mphantom></mphantom><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em">/</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\partial\hat{y}_{s}/\partial z_{si}=\alpha_{si}\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Gradient of PCC w.r.t. Attention Logits)<span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The derivative of Pearson correlation <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to a pre-softmax logit <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{si}</annotation></semantics></math> is</span></p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial z_{si}}=\frac{1}{S\sigma_{\hat{y}}}\left(\frac{a_{s}}{\sigma_{y}}-\rho\frac{b_{s}}{\sigma_{\hat{y}}}\right)\alpha_{si}\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mfrac><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial z_{si}}=\frac{1}{S\sigma_{\hat{y}}}\left(\frac{a_{s}}{\sigma_{y}}-\rho\frac{b_{s}}{\sigma_{\hat{y}}}\right)\alpha_{si}\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the interplay during joint optimization, we also examine the gradient of the MSE loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmlemma3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 2.3</span></span><span id="S2.Thmlemma3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Gradient of MSE w.r.t. Attention Logits)<span id="S2.Thmlemma3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmlemma3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.Thmlemma3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmlemma3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The derivative of MSE with respect to a pre-softmax logit <math id="S2.Thmlemma3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{si}</annotation></semantics></math> is</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</table>
</div>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Gradient Decomposition and the Optimization Conflict.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Comparing the PCC gradient (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Theorem 2.1 (Gradient of PCC w.r.t. Attention Logits). ‣ 2.3 Optimization Dynamics: The Correlation Gradient Bottleneck ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and the MSE gradient (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In Lemma 2.3 (Gradient of MSE w.r.t. Attention Logits). ‣ 2.3 Optimization Dynamics: The Correlation Gradient Bottleneck ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), we observe they share the same <em id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">local</em> structure factor <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{si}:=\alpha_{si}\,\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>α</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐰</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{si}:=\alpha_{si}\,\mathbf{w}^{\top}(\mathbf{h}_{si}-\mathbf{v}_{s})</annotation></semantics></math>, which governs attention adjustment within sample <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. The difference lies entirely in the <em id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">global</em> scaling factors which depend on overall batch statistics:</p>
</div>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The relative impact of MSE versus PCC optimization is determined by the ratio of these global factors. We analyze this ratio using their Root Mean Square (RMS) values across the batch.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(PCC/MSE Gradient Ratio Decay)<span id="S2.Thmcorollary1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Assuming <math id="S2.Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, the RMS ratio of the global scaling factors across the batch is bounded by:</span></p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{\mathrm{global}}:=\frac{\operatorname{RMS}_{s}(g_{s}^{\mathrm{PCC}})}{\operatorname{RMS}_{s}(g_{s}^{\mathrm{MSE}})}\leq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\sigma_{y}}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{\hat{y}}^{3/2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>global</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>RMS</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>PCC</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>RMS</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>MSE</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{\mathrm{global}}:=\frac{\operatorname{RMS}_{s}(g_{s}^{\mathrm{PCC}})}{\operatorname{RMS}_{s}(g_{s}^{\mathrm{MSE}})}\leq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\sigma_{y}}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sigma_{\hat{y}}^{3/2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Validation of gradient ratio (PCC/MSE) decay. The RMS ratio of PCC vs. MSE gradients (blue) is strictly constrained by the theoretical upper bound (red). The increase in prediction dispersion <math id="S2.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> (green) during training drives the attenuation of the PCC gradient signal relative to the MSE gradient.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17898v1/sigma_increase_temp.svg" id="S2.F4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:192/157;" width="192" height="157"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>The standard deviation of predictions <math id="S2.F4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\hat{y}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\hat{y}}</annotation></semantics></math> increases during training to match the standard deviation of labels <math id="S2.F4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{y}</annotation></semantics></math> under MSE loss.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S2.Thmcorollary1" title="Corollary 2.1 (PCC/MSE Gradient Ratio Decay). ‣ Gradient Decomposition and the Optimization Conflict. ‣ 2.3 Optimization Dynamics: The Correlation Gradient Bottleneck ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Corollary</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> identifies a gradient bottleneck where the PCC signal attenuates relative to MSE at a rate of <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}^{3/2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1/\sigma_{\hat{y}}^{3/2})</annotation></semantics></math>. This bound is empirically validated in <a href="#S2.F4" title="In Gradient Decomposition and the Optimization Conflict. ‣ 2.3 Optimization Dynamics: The Correlation Gradient Bottleneck ‣ 2 Theoretical Analysis of Correlation Learning in Attention-based Aggregation ‣ Breaking the Correlation Plateau: On the Optimization and Capacity Limits of Attention-Based Regressors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> on synthetic dataset , illustrating how magnitude matching dominates the optimization dynamics. We further analyze the magnitude of the PCC gradient alone, which reveals dependence on in-sample homogeneity.</p>
</div>

<div id="S2.Thmcorollary2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.Thmcorollary2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmcorollary2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The magnitude of the PCC gradient in <a href="#S2.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 2.1 (Gradient of PCC w.r.t.
